newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Japan MOF minister puts on the happy face roadshow.
newsitem.headline: Japan MOF minister puts on the happy face roadshow.

text.p: Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka put on a happy face and assured anyone who would listen at this weekend's APEC finance ministers' meeting that Japan's economy was sound and deregulation was under way.
Mitsuzuka arrived at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ministerial forum on Friday hot on the heels of U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's visit to Tokyo.
In Tokyo, Mitsuzuka had told Rubin that there was no need for concern over the Japanese trade surplus.
From the moment he stepped off the plane in Cebu to join Rubin at the APEC meeting, Mitsuzuka kept up his good news mantra.

Japan's trade surplus rose for the first time in two years in February, prompting warnings against its resurgence from U.S. officials, as the yen's weakness against the dollar helped make Japanese exports more competitive in world markets.
Mitsuzuka said he had told Rubin in Tokyo that Japan was pursuing economic recovery by boosting domestic demand, not exports.

Japanese officials said Mitsuzuka had made a "powerful" pitch to the APEC ministers at their Saturday session, repeating that Japan was on its way to recovery through domestic demand-led growth, and that this would be achieved through economic reforms.
At four of the seven bilateral meetings Mitsuzuka held on the fringe of the main forum, he volunteered the same, adding that foreigners need not worry over a banking crisis in Japan.
"Japanese banks have some bad loans, but you should not worry about a crisis," Mitsuzuka was quoted as telling Philippine President Fidel Ramos, who hosted the meeting on this luxury resort island.
He was referring to the restructuring announced last week of Nippon Credit Bank Ltd (8304.T) (NCB) and Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd (8312.T), the two Japanese banks worst hit by bad loan problems.
NCB, one of three long-term credit banks in Japan, announced it would write off bad loans totalling 460 billion yen, as well as sell off its Tokyo headquarters and withdraw from overseas operation.
Hokkaido Takushoku, one of Japan's top 20 city banks, also announced last week that it was withdrawing from overseas operations and merging with a smaller regional bank.
In meetings with International Monetary Fund managing director Michel Camdessus and the finance ministers of Australia, South Korea and the Philippines, Mitsuzuka kept up the economic cheer.

In case anybody had failed to get the message, Mitsuzuka devoted most of his closing news conference to the same theme, including calling reporters back at the end of the conference to tell them one more time.
"Members of the foreign press corps," he said. "Our nation's economy will be led by domestic demand, not exports."
